1.pericope_label: In my distress I cried unto the Lord, and he heard me... Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper

schools.summary: Delitzsch links this first song of degrees to the closing verse of the psalm before it and leaves the period open, noting a proposal that the collection belongs to the years after the Return; Ellicott generalizes the complaint to the nation under foreign rule and reads the third verse rhetorically, as asking what further epithet could be added to a tongue already called lying.

Gill traces the lying lips through Doeg, Saul's courtiers, the Pharisees and the false witnesses, and prefers to read the arrows and coals as the Lord's punishment rather than as a picture of the tongue; Calvin will not affirm the authorship but finds David's manner throughout, and takes the fourth verse as comparison rather than sentence.

Clarke works through the title, rejecting the fifteen temple steps for want of evidence and assigning the collection to the returning exiles by an unknown and probably plural hand; Wesley reads the arrows flatly as the vengeance of God.

Henry divides the injury into lies told to David and lies told of him, and takes the fourth verse as the wrath of God reaching from afar; Spurgeon measures the wound slander makes and counsels silence toward men and prayer toward God.
Augustine reads the degrees as a ladder used in both directions, and holds that suffering the tongues of adversaries is the mark of having begun to ascend at all.

debates.question: Who wrote the psalm, and when?

positions.view: David, on the evidence of style, though the name is not given.
Probably during or after the Babylonian captivity, by an unknown hand, and the collection probably not by one author at all.
The period is uncertain; a proposal placing these songs after the Return, against Samaritan hostility, deserves recording.

debates.question: Do the sharp arrows and coals describe the slanderous tongue or its punishment?

positions.view: The punishment God will inflict on the calumniator.
A comparison for calumny itself, which pierces like an arrow and burns long like these coals.
The stock figures of malicious speech, supplied as the answer to a rhetorical question about epithets.

outliers.note: Alone reads the title as a ladder with a downward as well as an upward use, those who have understanding descending to feed infants with milk.
Corrects the plant to broom, describes the Arab charcoal trade in it, and files the year-old embers among the wonderful stories told by Jerome and the rabbis.

themes: In my distress I cried unto the Lord, and he heard me.
Deliver my soul, O Lord, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue.
What shall be given unto thee? or what shall be done unto thee, thou false tongue?
Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper.

5.pericope_label: Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar!... I am for peace: but when I speak, they are for war

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the very remoteness of the two peoples the reason for pairing them, one savage type from the north and one from the south, and allows that the poet may have been veiling an allusion to real tribes; his note on the closing verse survives only as a fragment.

Gill weighs the candidates for Meshech and prefers the Cappadocians, and turns the sixth verse into a chain of everything the peace-hater hates; Calvin defends the word as a proper name against the ancient versions, then holds that under it the psalmist means his own countrymen, and presses that speaking here amounts to offering terms of peace.

Clarke keeps the names geographical and follows Calmet in locating them among the peoples that held Jewish exiles, describing the enemies as a marauding tent-dwelling people who would hear of nothing but their old manner of life; Wesley takes the names metaphorically on the ground that the next verse explains them.

Henry denies that David ever lived in either country, compares the idiom to saying of bad neighbours that we dwell among Turks and heathens, and finds a double grief in banishment from the ordinances and in the company of the wicked.

debates.question: Are Meshech and Kedar literal places of residence?

positions.view: No; the names are metaphors for rude neighbours, as the next verse shows.
Yes; they are the regions that held Jewish captives, and the psalm is the exiles' complaint.
They are types of savagery chosen from north and south for their very remoteness, possibly veiling a real allusion.
The identification of Meshech is itself unsettled, and the likeliest candidate is chosen by nearness to Judea.

debates.question: Is the trouble an individual's or the nation's?

positions.view: David's own, in Saul's court or among false brethren of his own people.
The whole nation's; the closing verses leave no doubt of it.
The captives' collectively, against the tribes among whom they were held.

outliers.note: Argues the philology for a proper name against the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate and Arabic, which all render the word as an appellative meaning a protracted sojourn.
Identifies the enemies concretely as tent-dwelling Arabs subsisting by plunder, with the captives vainly urging them to take up the arts of peace.

themes: Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar!
My soul hath long dwelt with him that hateth peace.
I am for peace: but when I speak, they are for war.
